newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Iraq news hits oil prices as OPEC gathers.
newsitem.headline: Iraq news hits oil prices as OPEC gathers.

text.p: The prospect of the United Nations easing its Gulf War ban on Iraqi oil exports could halt this year's surprise world oil price rally, oil experts said on Tuesday.

But while that would bring relief to consumers, the view on Tuesday as OPEC oil ministers assembled for a conference in Vienna was that strong winter demand for fuel meant that the market was not about to collapse suddenly.
Iraq's U.N. ambassador, Nizar Hamdoon, said on Monday that Iraq agreed to conditions that had delayed a pact to let it export oil for the first time since it invaded Kuwait in 1990.
The accord, designed to help it buy food and medicine, had been shelved in September when President Saddam Hussein sent troops to north Iraq to intervene in Kurdish faction fighting.
Benchmark light crude oil, lately on a strong rally, fell 42 cents to end Monday at $22.61 per barrel on the Hamdoon news. But traders said it held support at around that value.
"The market is hungry for barrels right now," said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk for brokers Smith Barney.
The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) begins a scheduled twice-yearly conference on Wednesday.
Ministers had already pencilled in a possible revival of sales from founder-member Iraq to their production quota system when they last met in June.

The OPEC problem is that several of the 11 cartel members are cheating on their mandated quotas, and total OPEC daily volume is already almost a million barrels above the intended ceiling of 25.03 million -- even before Iraqi exports flow.
Violations by members like Venezuela are unlikely to stop, delegates said.

But they added that OPEC is most likely to extend quotas until June 30, 1997, and hope for some restraint to prevent too rapid an erosion of prices early next year when peak cold weather fuel demand is over and Iraq may be back.
"It's cold and I hope it gets colder," says OPEC Secretary-General Rilwanu Lukman of Nigeria.
Cartel president, Rakad bin Salem bin Rakad of the United Arab Emirates, told reporters in Vienna that Iraq would be no problem "on condition each member of OPEC will be restricted to their quota".
Hamdoon said in New York that Iraqi oil could flow as soon as December under the accord to permit sales worth $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicine.
But the deal has repeatedly been held up and sceptical traders noted that technical details including a pricing formula had yet to be finalised.

OPEC's solace -- if Iraq really is about to return to the market -- is that prices are riding high. An average of almost $20 per barrel so far this year is up $3 from 1995 and is the firmest since the Gulf War.
Higher prices added a windfall extra $30 billion in 1996 revenues for the OPEC exporters whose economies were crimped in recent years when oil languished in the bargain basement.
Saudi Arabia, for instance, which produces a third of all cartel oil, can expect $10 billion of excess to deal with a projected 1996 deficit of almost $5 billion.
